Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 156 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Background 
Aerial surveys are conducted periodically to obtain current big game population estimates, which assist biologists 
with species management decisions.  Wildlife Management Unit 156 is located in the Strathmore, AB area and 
comprises mostly annually cropped agricul tural private land with numerous riparian watercourse running easterly, 
with the Bow and Red Deer Rivers on the south and north west boundaries.  Current hunting regulations in place 
include: General License White -tailed Deer, Special License Mule Deer, Sp ecial License Elk, and Special License 
Moose at harvests levels consistent with species management plans which maximizes hunter opportunity. It was last 
surveyed for mule and white -tailed deer in 2001. Chronic Wasting Disease has been detected in WMU 156 a s of 
2017. 
 
Survey method 
Distance sampling methodology (Buckland et al. 2001) was used in order to complete a multispecies big game 
survey of WMU 156, excluding Siksika Nation, with transects spaced at 1 minute of latitude,  The survey was flown 
on Jan 13, 14, 15, 16th with crew (G Chapman, B Boukall, J Nicholson, and K Morton and pilot G Goodison/Ascent 
Helicopters).  A total of 22.1 hours was used to complete this survey.  WMU 156 is 4068 km2 in area and a total 
survey effort of 2198 km of transect was  flown.  Survey conditions were excellent snow cover and daily high 
temperatures of -26 to -31, and nightly lows to -35 degree C with overcast to clear skies and no wind. 
 
Results 
A total of 116 groups of mule deer, 95 groups of white-tailed deer, 36 groups of moose were observed, while no elk 
groups  or tracks were detected.  The population estimates for mule deer and white -tailed deer were 2,588 and 
2,309, respectively (Table 1). To enhance survey efficiency, not all deer groups were classified, with a to tal of 63 
groups (640 total) mule deer and 34 groups (342 total) white-tailed deer classified (Figure 1) according to department 
aerial survey protocol (AEP 2020).  The buck:doe:fawn ratio was for 49:100:64 for mule deer and 28:100:64 for 
white-tailed deer.   
 
These results indicate that mule deer populations are similar to when surveyed in 2001 when the mule deer 
population was estimated to be 2893 animals (AEP 2020b).  White -tailed deer populations have increased 
considerably since last estimated at 1040 animals in 2001, however, it is recognized that historical estimates for 
white-tailed deer may have been limited by survey analysis and design capabilities at that time. A total of 20 cows, 
9 calves, and 15 bull moose were observed.  Moose have never been surveyed in this WMU however, a pre-hunting 
season moose estimate of 100 -125 animals has been estimated since 2013, and supports a harvest of ~10 cows 
and ~10 bulls annually. Most moose were associated with the Rosebud River and other riparian/coulee tributaries of 
the Red Deer River. An additional 219 coyotes, 1 covey of sharp-tailed grouse, 1 red fox, and 1 new great blue heron 
rookery were also noted.
